item.title: VLM4S: A Vision‐Language Model Framework for Geographically and Environmentally Informed Soundscape Assessment
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 6, September 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Sound environments shape urban experience, yet conventional noise monitoring relies on isolated sensors lacking semantic context and spatial scalability. In this study, we develop a Vision‐Language Model for Soundscape (VLM4S), an exploratory, sensor‐free framework for inferring acoustic conditions from street‐view imagery. This framework addresses three tasks: identifying visible sound sources, predicting sound pressure levels (SPL), and classifying sound types (Natural/Mechanical/Human‐made). Utilizing a small‐scale experimental dataset of 200 co‐located training pairs, 20 pilot validation samples, and 40 out‐of‐sample test cases spanning eleven cities globally, we evaluate whether a vision‐language foundation model can utilize its pre‐trained visual knowledge to estimate real‐world environmental sound levels. The fine‐tuned model achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 5.4 dB on the pilot validation set. Ablation analysis reveals that integrating street‐view imagery and Mel‐spectrograms with a Chain‐of‐Thought (CoT) prompt achieves the lowest error (MAE=5.9dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=5.9\ \mathrm{dB} $$), outperforming pure visual scrutiny (MAE=12.4dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=12.4\ \mathrm{dB} $$) and direct prediction without CoT (MAE=9.8dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=9.8\ \mathrm{dB} $$). External comparisons against United States Department of Transportation annual noise maps across 4000+ Manhattan locations reveal a moderate spatial correlation (r=0.504$$ r=0.504 $$, MAE=9.1dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=9.1\ \mathrm{dB} $$, Bias=+6.7dB$$ \mathrm{Bias}=+6.7\ \mathrm{dB} $$). While output discretization limits this generative approach for strict regulatory use, the framework provides a highly sample‐efficient baseline for exploratory soundscape assessment and hotspot identification in data‐scarce regions.

ABSTRACT

Sound environments shape urban experience, yet conventional noise monitoring relies on isolated sensors lacking semantic context and spatial scalability. In this study, we develop a Vision-Language Model for Soundscape (VLM4S), an exploratory, sensor-free framework for inferring acoustic conditions from street-view imagery. This framework addresses three tasks: identifying visible sound sources, predicting sound pressure levels (SPL), and classifying sound types (Natural/Mechanical/Human-made). Utilizing a small-scale experimental dataset of 200 co-located training pairs, 20 pilot validation samples, and 40 out-of-sample test cases spanning eleven cities globally, we evaluate whether a vision-language foundation model can utilize its pre-trained visual knowledge to estimate real-world environmental sound levels. The fine-tuned model achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 5.4 dB on the pilot validation set. Ablation analysis reveals that integrating street-view imagery and Mel-spectrograms with a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt achieves the lowest error (MAE=5.9dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=5.9\ \mathrm{dB} $$), outperforming pure visual scrutiny (MAE=12.4dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=12.4\ \mathrm{dB} $$) and direct prediction without CoT (MAE=9.8dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=9.8\ \mathrm{dB} $$). External comparisons against United States Department of Transportation annual noise maps across 4000+ Manhattan locations reveal a moderate spatial correlation (r=0.504$$ r=0.504 $$, MAE=9.1dB$$ \mathrm{MAE}=9.1\ \mathrm{dB} $$, Bias=+6.7dB$$ \mathrm{Bias}=+6.7\ \mathrm{dB} $$). While output discretization limits this generative approach for strict regulatory use, the framework provides a highly sample-efficient baseline for exploratory soundscape assessment and hotspot identification in data-scarce regions.

item.title: Polyhedral Reconstruction of Advanced 3D Building Geometries by Data Fusion and Polygon Covering in Urban Areas
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 6, September 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT This paper presents several enhancements to the universal generation of realistic 3D urban scenes with detailed roof shapes, leveraging key data sources such as OpenStreetMap and Digital Terrain Models. The prior approach relied on core principles of 3D mesh generation, producing models compatible with various 3D rendering systems and game engines. In this study, cadastral data is employed to automatically determine the number of building levels, utilizing datasets from the Spanish Virtual Cadastral Office for this determination. The proposed reconstruction method successfully processes approximately 97% of OpenStreetMap building entities that include valid roof definitions. A polygon‐covering algorithm was implemented to generate volumetric models for buildings with complex footprints and representative roof shapes. In future work, the capacity of this algorithm and the quality of the terrain models can still be improved.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

This paper presents several enhancements to the universal generation of realistic 3D urban scenes with detailed roof shapes, leveraging key data sources such as OpenStreetMap and Digital Terrain Models. The prior approach relied on core principles of 3D mesh generation, producing models compatible with various 3D rendering systems and game engines. In this study, cadastral data is employed to automatically determine the number of building levels, utilizing datasets from the Spanish Virtual Cadastral Office for this determination. The proposed reconstruction method successfully processes approximately 97% of OpenStreetMap building entities that include valid roof definitions. A polygon-covering algorithm was implemented to generate volumetric models for buildings with complex footprints and representative roof shapes. In future work, the capacity of this algorithm and the quality of the terrain models can still be improved.
